sentences.text: The single known individual of Sciurumimus is a juvenile measuring about 72 centimeters in length, possessing a skull that is 156% the size of its femur.
Filamentous feathers covered the base of the tail and other body parts, creating a shaggy look similar to skin.
Its forelimbs were short and robust, featuring three long-toed segments with claws making up roughly 45% of the leg length, while the tail contained a total of 59 vertebrae.
Although most soft tissue remains are feathers, a small area of what might be muscle tissue is visible along the back edge of the shin bone.
Dating back approximately 151 million years, this fossil is regarded as one of the most well-preserved dinosaur remains globally.
The skull is exceptionally large for the animal, exceeding the length of the entire series of neck vertebrae.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as BMMS BK 11, was unearthed between 2009 and 2010 at limestone quarries near Painten in southern Germany.
Excavations were financed by dealer Raimund Albersdörfer, and his wife Birgit donated the find to the Solnhofen Mayor-Müller Museum as a permanent loan.
Although informally announced in 2011, the species was not officially named and described until 2012 by Rauhut and colleagues.
Dietary adaptations are visible in the teeth, where the first four upper jaw teeth lack serrations while the remaining 33 to 35 teeth have backward-pointing serrated edges.
It is likely that young animals consumed different food sources than their adult counterparts.
Adults probably grew to a body length of 5 meters and may have shown signs of insular dwarfism.
The species is currently classified within the superfamily Megalosauroidea, a grouping listed by the Paleobiology Database.
Early phylogenetic studies suggested it was a primitive member of Megalosauroidea, a clade of large, early carnivorous dinosaurs.
Later work by Foth and colleagues tentatively placed the animal in Megalosauroidea again in 2020, this time alongside Juravenator.
Sciurumimus lived during the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic, roughly 150 million years ago in what is now Europe.
Initial analyses faced criticism because the data matrices used to link the new fossil were incomplete and missing information from several species.
Some studies found the animal to be a compsognathid, though researchers noted this placement was tentative.
Other investigations suggested it was an allosauroid or a tetanuran located outside the Avetheropoda group.
In 2016, Paul positioned Sciurumimus as a basal member among the Maniraptoromorpha.
